title: The yes–no bias of large language models reflects answer order and wording, not shifts in moral judgment

bias_targets.methodology: Using a psychometric battery with crossed symmetrization across logically equivalent question forms to measure how models' binary verdicts on moral dilemmas shift based on irrelevant framing changes.

Crossing the question's verb (e.g., approve/oppose) with the printed order of the answer options (e.g., yes-first/no-first) to isolate and measure the model's pull toward the last-printed option (recency bias).

Replacing standard 'yes/no' answer words with arbitrary labels (e.g., A/B), quasi-lexical marks (e.g., True/False, thumbs up/down), or non-lexical symbols to measure the model's attraction to the specific word 'no' independent of the actual semantic verdict.
Evaluating if a model has a verdict-attached preference (a disposition to reject/oppose) by separating the verdict meaning from the surface formatting using arbitrary answer labels.
